africa.headline: Cyberattacks turned October into a costly month for Nigerian banks
africa.teaser: Wave of attacks caused significant fraud losses in customer funds.
africa.whyItMatters: Highlights critical vulnerability of financial infrastructure in the region.
africa.bankAngle: Urgent need for enhanced cybersecurity and fraud prevention protocols.
africa.imageAlt: Cyberattacks turned October into a costly month for Nigerian banks
africa.longSummary:
## The story
In early October 2026, a wave of cyberattacks struck several Nigerian banks and financial institutions, potentially placing billions of naira in customer funds at risk, according to sources cited by TechCabal. The incidents hit institutions that rely on external technology providers to operate critical financial services, including core banking infrastructure. One vendor that supplies core banking services to multiple financial institutions was reportedly compromised at the system level on October 1. TechCabal described the vendor as one of Africa’s largest fintech companies but did not name it. The outlet said it could not immediately establish how many attacks occurred, how much money was lost, or whether the incidents were connected.

A senior executive at a payment gateway, who asked not to be named, described October as “Black October” and said the attacks affected businesses across the financial services industry. Another source at an investment bank said staff were warned not to open external emails amid heightened cyber threats during the month. A major microfinance bank was also among the affected institutions, according to a source familiar with the incident. That bank reportedly suffered financial losses and system disruption, forcing it to seek temporary alternatives to keep services running; it has since hired a chief security officer.

Adedeji Olowe, founder and CEO of Nigerian lending technology company Lendsqr, told TechCabal that “everyone has been attacked” and that people have lost money. In a LinkedIn post on November 4, Olowe said security testing of Lendsqr’s platform uncovered about 800 vulnerabilities and that his team spent three weeks fixing them. He did not disclose the vulnerabilities’ severity, how many were fixed, or whether any were exploited. NIBSS did not respond to TechCabal’s request for comment.

## Key details
TechCabal reported that three of Nigeria’s largest banks—Access Holdings Plc, Guaranty Trust Holding Company Plc (GTCO), and Zenith Bank—collectively reported ₦2.74 billion (about $2.03 million) in fraud losses for the first six months of 2026. GTCO recorded the sharpest year-on-year increase, with fraud losses up 450.24 percent.

The Financial Institutions Training Centre (FITC) reported 19,719 fraud cases in the fourth quarter of 2025, a 34.2 percent increase from the previous quarter. Reported fraud losses in that quarter surged 575.7 percent to ₦5.26 billion (about $3.89 million). NIBSS data cited in the article shows financial institutions recorded ₦25.85 billion (about $19.16 million) in actual fraud losses for all of 2025, a 50.55 percent decline from 2024. However, the proportion of attempted frauds that resulted in losses rose from 60.53 percent in 2024 to 68.81 percent in 2025.

The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) told TechCabal it maintains ongoing supervisory oversight of cybersecurity incidents affecting regulated institutions and that the financial system remains resilient. Under its 2024 Risk-Based Cybersecurity Framework, the CBN requires banks and payment service banks to assess third-party providers through due diligence, routine audits, and ongoing monitoring. The framework requires supervised institutions to report detected cyber incidents within 24 hours and submit monthly threat intelligence. In March 2026, the CBN formally recognized artificial intelligence as a tool for fighting financial crime.

The CBN’s Payment System Vision 2028 identifies rising SIM swap incidents, account takeover fraud, insider collusion, and social engineering as key risks. It proposes a national Security Operations Centre and a fraud intelligence-sharing platform, with a broader goal of reducing fraud losses by 70 percent by 2028. The CBN has also directed NIBSS to debit the settlement accounts of commercial banks that receive fraud proceeds, a rule intended to make institutions tighten fraud detection.

The article notes significant reporting gaps. NIBSS’s 2023 Annual Fraud Landscape found that only 60 of 163 profiled financial institutions reported fraud incidents that year, a 37 percent compliance rate; the remaining 103 did not report cases. The article also references a December 2024 TechCabal report that First Bank lost ₦7 billion (about $5.19 million) to fraud, and that an employee diverted ₦60 billion (about $44.47 million) over two years undetected, leading to more than 100 dismissals.

## Why it matters
The October attacks illustrate how a breach at one shared technology provider can expose multiple banks simultaneously. Because many Nigerian financial institutions depend on the same vendors for core banking, payment processing, and lending infrastructure, a single compromise can ripple across the system instead of staying contained at one institution.

For a product team at a bank, the episode reinforces the need for rigorous vendor risk management, rapid incident reporting, and strong customer-facing fraud controls. The CBN’s 2024 framework already requires third-party due diligence and disclosure of cyber incidents within 24 hours, but the article suggests compliance is uneven across the industry. NIBSS data indicates that although total fraud losses fell in 2025, a larger share of attempted fraud is succeeding, which points to evolving attacker methods rather than a diminishing threat.

The article also references prior losses at First Bank, showing that threats come from outside actors and insiders alike. The CBN’s directive to debit settlement accounts of banks that receive fraud proceeds shifts more accountability to financial institutions for transaction monitoring. Whether these measures reduce losses will depend on how quickly institutions detect incidents, disclose them to regulators, and share intelligence with peers.

africa.headline: Microsoft outage pushes Kenya’s banks onto WhatsApp and phone lines
africa.teaser: Global server failure exposes heavy reliance on single US provider.
africa.whyItMatters: Demonstrates systemic risk of cloud dependency.
africa.bankAngle: Banks must diversify cloud infrastructure to ensure operational resilience.
africa.imageAlt: Microsoft outage pushes Kenya’s banks onto WhatsApp and phone lines
africa.longSummary:
## The story

On Thursday afternoon, a global Microsoft 365 outage disrupted email and associated services for several of Kenya’s largest banks, just as the workday was beginning in Nairobi. Microsoft first acknowledged mailbox problems shortly before 1 PM New York time, which corresponded to 9 PM in Nairobi, the hour when Old Mutual’s Kenyan unit reported its email going down. By Friday, Equity Bank, Stanbic Bank Kenya, Standard Chartered Bank Kenya, UBA Kenya, and Loop, NCBA Group’s digital bank, had all instructed customers to reach them via WhatsApp, phone lines, or call centres. Equity and UBA specifically cited a global service disruption affecting Microsoft Outlook; Standard Chartered told customers only that its email was unavailable; Loop said both its email and in-app support channels were down. Insurers Old Mutual Kenya and APA Insurance also reported losing email access, with APA additionally losing SharePoint and OneDrive. Other businesses, including a Nairobi‑based security agency and a travel agency, redirected clients to phone lines and social media. Notably, none of the banks’ public notices mentioned problems with payments or mobile banking services. Microsoft attributed the disruption to a large number of servers becoming unexpectedly unavailable, which increased load on the rest of its infrastructure, and said it saw no sign of a cyberattack. Downdetector tracked the outage across 74 countries and territories. By Friday morning, Microsoft stated that service capacity had not yet returned to normal levels and had not provided an estimate for full recovery.

## Key details

The banks most directly affected span Kenya’s major lenders. TechCabal reports Equity serves 23.3 million customers and processes 89.7 % of its transactions on digital platforms, and it asked customers to call or message it on WhatsApp. Stanbic Bank Kenya, a subsidiary of South Africa’s Standard Bank Group, directed customers to its Voice Branch call centre or their relationship managers. Standard Chartered Bank Kenya, majority‑owned by London‑based Standard Chartered (which holds 73.89 % of its Kenyan unit), told customers by text that its email service was unavailable. UBA Kenya, part of Nigeria’s UBA Group that operates across 20 African countries as well as in the US, the UK, France, and the United Arab Emirates, named Microsoft Outlook as the cause and offered phone lines, a WhatsApp number, and relationship manager contacts. Loop, NCBA Group’s digital‑only bank, confirmed that both its email and in‑app support channels were down and pointed customers to phone lines and social media. Beyond banks, Old Mutual Kenya apologised to customers after losing email access, while APA Insurance lost email as well as Microsoft’s SharePoint and OneDrive, according to an email seen by TechCabal. Securex Agencies, a Nairobi security firm founded in 1970, and a local travel agency also shifted communications to phone lines and social media. Across all notices, no bank or insurer reported disruptions to payment systems or mobile banking channels.

## Why it matters

The outage exposed the extent to which Kenya’s financial sector depends on a single foreign cloud provider for everyday operational tools. Even as lenders have moved most customer business into digital channels, their internal email, document storage, and support systems remain hosted on Microsoft 365, with few immediate local alternatives. The stalled $1 billion Microsoft and G42 data centre project, intended to bring an Azure cloud region to East Africa, was halted when the Kenyan government declined the payment guarantees the companies sought; officials have since said the project remains on track, but the incident underscores the limited domestic capacity to host critical services. East Africa’s live data‑centre load stood at roughly 30 megawatts in 2025, according to industry estimates, and a local data centre would not necessarily have shielded users, given that Microsoft runs its email and file services on shared global infrastructure. The event is the latest in a series of Microsoft 365 disruptions this year, including outages in January and July, and a late‑August incident that locked thousands of users worldwide out of their mailboxes. For an industry that processes millions of transactions daily, the outage illustrates how an upstream cloud failure can cascade into an operational continuity crisis, even when core payment rails remain functional. It also raises questions about resilience planning, diversification of technology providers, and the readiness of fallback channels such as WhatsApp and phone lines to sustain customer service during prolonged infrastructure failures.

africa.headline: The bank OPay hoped would open up Africa
africa.teaser: Platform moves money and extends credit, heavily concentrated in Nigeria.
africa.whyItMatters: Key player in African digital financial inclusion.
africa.bankAngle: Example of a dominant regional player scaling financial services.
africa.imageAlt: The bank OPay hoped would open up Africa
africa.longSummary:
## The story
OPay, a Nigerian-dominant fintech, sought to expand across Africa by partnering with Standard Bank Group, Africa’s largest bank by assets. On October 9, 2026, Standard Bank agreed to invest approximately $185 million in OPay, with its Africa head, Lungisa Fuzile, joining OPay’s board of directors. The investment was conditional on OPay completing a New York Stock Exchange initial public offering and receiving applicable regulatory approvals. Beyond capital, the companies intended to explore digital banking and the distribution of selected Standard Bank products and services through OPay’s consumer and merchant platform. However, on October 30, 2026, OPay withdrew its planned NYSE listing following a reported regulatory inquiry from China. The failed IPO has raised questions about what OPay could lose from a partnership that promised access to banking infrastructure, regulatory relationships, and financial products needed to expand across Africa.

## Key details
OPay’s revenue is 89.5% concentrated in Nigeria, which the company says presents a problem for a fintech seeking to become a pan-African financial services business. Standard Bank’s investment of roughly $185 million was tied to OPay’s IPO success and regulatory clearance; Lungisa Fuzile, head of Standard Bank Group’s Africa operations, was set to sit on OPay’s board. The collaboration was non-binding and did not oblige either company to implement specific initiatives. OPay’s typical market-entry model involves identifying local payment pain points, acquiring licensed partners or obtaining banking licenses, and replicating its stack of digital payments, savings, and consumer credit. Standard Bank operates across 21 African markets, including Angola, Botswana, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Ghana, Mozambique, and Zambia. GSMA 2024 data shows digital merchant payment penetration at 19.2% in Zambia, 18.5% in Mozambique, and 27.3% in Ghana, markets OPay identified as having clear unmet need and a path to build its full model. OPay reports over 50.1 million monthly active users and offers digital payments, savings, consumer lending, and merchant financial services. The proposed collaboration could have allowed Standard Bank’s selected products–such as savings and investment tools, additional lending, insurance, and remittance services–to be distributed through OPay’s platform, expanding the range of financial products available to OPay’s customers without the fintech developing every offering independently. Nigeria received $20.93 billion in personal remittances in 2024 according to the Central Bank of Nigeria; Standard Bank’s international banking relationships and African footprint could have enabled OPay to participate more deeply in last-mile distribution of cross-border payments. OPay withdrew its NYSE listing on October 30, 2026, following a reported regulatory inquiry from China, undermining the IPO-conditioned Standard Bank deal.

## Why it matters
The OPay-Standard Bank collaboration illustrated a strategic pathway for fast-growing fintechs to overcome African market-entry barriers by leveraging established banks’ regulatory expertise, banking infrastructure, and continental footprint. For OPay, the partnership could have accelerated diversification beyond Nigeria’s 89.5% revenue concentration, tapped underpenetrated markets where digital merchant payments range from 18% to 27%, and expanded its product suite via Standard Bank’s existing offerings–savings, lending, insurance, and remittances–without full independent development. For Standard Bank, OPay’s digital network offered a route to distribute selected financial services to consumers and merchants underserved by conventional banking. The IPO withdrawal, triggered by a Chinese regulatory inquiry, demonstrates how geopolitical and regulatory headwinds can dismantle cross-border fintech partnerships even after public announcement, particularly when investments are conditional on public market events. The outcome underscores the risk that financing structures tied to IPO timelines can create fragility in strategic alliances. Moving forward, OPay may need to rely on acquisitions, local licensing, and direct regulatory engagement to replicate its model across Africa, while Standard Bank may seek alternative distribution channels or adjust its fintech partnership strategy. The episode offers a case study in the complexities of scaling financial technology across diverse African regulatory environments, where banking infrastructure, local partnerships, and capital market access remain decisive factors for expansion.

africa.headline: Rand stablecoins gain checkout traction on MoneyBadger network
africa.teaser: Monthly checkout value doubled as stablecoins compete for retail payments.
africa.whyItMatters: Growth in digital asset adoption for retail commerce.
africa.bankAngle: Stablecoins are becoming a viable alternative for retail payment processing.
africa.imageAlt: Rand stablecoins gain checkout traction on MoneyBadger network
africa.longSummary:
## The story

South Africa’s MoneyBadger payment network is showing measurable traction for rand-denominated stablecoins at retail checkout. In September 2026, ZARU — issued by BlockTower South Africa under Financial Sector Conduct Authority (FSCA) licence FSP 55172 — recorded R1.28 million in checkout value, a 2.64-fold increase from June’s R484,207. The growth curve has not flattened; September ran 10.6% ahead of August. A smaller rival, ZARsc, issued by Supercoin under FSCA licence FSP 53458 and backed by NYSE-listed Super Group, posted R4,408 in September checkout value, up 286.9% from August’s low base, with R40,216 cumulative through September. Both tokens operate on a network where total payment volume nearly doubled in the first half of 2026 versus the same period in 2025, overall rand value grew 176%, and active merchant locations expanded from 57 to 2,927 year-over-year.

The checkout data reveals a practical use case rather than speculative activity. Half of all payments on the network are under R200, and 87% are under R1,000. The median scan-to-paid time was 35 seconds or less in an August 2026 benchmark. For low-value, high-frequency retail transactions, price volatility is a functional problem, which gives rand-pegged instruments an advantage over Bitcoin at the till. In the 2026 year-to-date breakdown, Bitcoin accounted for 39.9% of checkout spending, USDT for 36.1%, and ZARU for 7.7%. Combined, the two rand stablecoins represented roughly 44% of total transaction value, a figure the network says reflects payment use rather than trading.

ZARU’s institutional architecture is deliberate. Launched in February 2026 through a consortium that includes BlockTower, Luno, EasyEquities, Lesaka, and Sanlam Specialised Asset Management, the token’s rand reserves are managed by Sanlam and held at Standard Bank and Absa. Moore Johannesburg conducts monthly agreed-upon procedures on those reserves, with reports published publicly. Qualified clients can mint and redeem directly through BlockTower’s issuance platform. ZARsc, by contrast, has prioritized exchange listings in its first year — VALR, Luno, OVEX, and the Solana-based Orca — with a consumer wallet planned for early 2027. Both issuers operate as licensed Crypto Asset Service Providers under the FSCA framework, which brought crypto assets under the Financial Advisory and Intermediary Services Act. The regulator does not grant these tokens legal tender status; they remain digital assets, and redemption into bank funds depends on each issuer’s channels.

## Key details

ZARU’s growth has been catalyzed by a cashback campaign run through Luno Pay and expanding workplace adoption perks, according to MoneyBadger data. BlockTower’s chief commercial officer, Aleks Andjelopolj, said the adoption figures illustrate how institutions can build rewards programmes and employee perks on top of the stablecoin infrastructure, framing it as an invitation to fintech, domestic payment, capital market, cross-border settlement, and retail institutions. The merchant model MoneyBadger operates keeps foreign-currency exposure off the merchant’s balance sheet: stores receive rand settlement regardless of which token the customer tenders. This sidesteps the foreign-exchange risk and regulatory friction that dollar stablecoins introduce for South African consumers and merchants settling in rand.

Globally, US dollar stablecoins dominate retail and institutional flows, with USDT and USDC commanding the vast majority of stablecoin transaction volume. Rand-denominated instruments face a structurally smaller addressable market, but they address a specific local friction: the need to convert dollar stablecoins into rand for settlement, which adds cost, delay, and regulatory complexity. The MoneyBadger network’s ability to settle merchants in rand instantly, irrespective of the token used, removes that friction at the point of sale. The network’s transaction profile — small ticket sizes, sub-minute settlement — aligns with everyday retail rather than wholesale or speculative flows.

The next milestones to watch are the rollout of Supercoin’s consumer wallet in early 2027, the expansion of Luno Pay’s cashback campaigns to additional retail partners, and whether ZARU’s planned launches across other African and Asia-Pacific markets add cross-border settlement volumes to the retail numbers already on the board. ZARsc’s exchange-first strategy may shift as the consumer wallet launches, potentially broadening its retail footprint. Both tokens remain subject to FSCA oversight as Crypto Asset Service Providers, a category that has gained clearer definition in South Africa but does not equate to legal tender status.

## Why it matters

The data suggests a viable retail payment rail for rand stablecoins is emerging in South Africa, distinct from the dollar-stablecoin dominance seen globally. The combination of institutional-grade reserve management, regulatory licensing, and a merchant settlement model that absorbs currency risk creates a template that could be replicated in other emerging markets where local-currency settlement is a prerequisite for merchant adoption. The 44% stablecoin share of checkout value on MoneyBadger, driven largely by USDT but with rand tokens gaining, indicates that merchants and consumers will use stablecoins for payments when volatility is removed and settlement is instant in the local currency.

For banks and payment incumbents, the development signals that stablecoin infrastructure is moving beyond wholesale and cross-border use cases into everyday retail. The consortium behind ZARU includes asset managers, exchanges, and investment platforms, showing how traditional financial institutions can participate without directly issuing tokens. The workplace perks and cashback mechanics demonstrate how stablecoins can be embedded into existing loyalty and payroll flows, potentially accelerating adoption without requiring consumers to understand blockchain mechanics.

The regulatory clarity provided by the FSCA’s Crypto Asset Service Provider framework appears to be a necessary condition for this growth. Both issuers operate under licences that impose reserve transparency, audit requirements, and consumer protection obligations. However, the framework’s limitation — tokens are not legal tender and redemption depends on issuer channels — means systemic risk remains contained but also that interoperability with the broader banking system relies on bilateral arrangements. As ZARU expands into other African and Asia-Pacific markets, the test will be whether the same institutional architecture and merchant settlement model can scale across jurisdictions with different regulatory regimes and currency environments.

ghana.headline: MTN Ghana targets 1 million homes for fibre connectivity
ghana.teaser: Network expansion aims to support growing demand for AI and digital connectivity.
ghana.whyItMatters: Critical infrastructure for digital economy growth.
ghana.imageAlt: MTN Ghana targets 1 million homes for fibre connectivity
ghana.longSummary:
## The story

MTN Ghana has announced a plan to extend its Fibre-to-the-Home network to one million homes over the next three years. According to Techfocus24, the target was disclosed by Chief Executive Officer Stephen Blewett at the company’s 2026 Vendor Conference. The company presents the expansion as part of a broader effort to strengthen infrastructure for rising demand for digital connectivity and emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence.

The announcement also ties the fibre buildout to MTN Ghana’s preparation for 5G services. Blewett said the company intends to use its 5G licence to offer more modern connectivity and improved internet speeds. In that context, the FTTH programme is described as a significant undertaking that will depend on vendors and partners.

A second theme in the article is vendor governance. MTN Ghana’s leadership used the conference to emphasize trust, transparency, accountability and shared objectives. Chief Financial Officer Antoinette Kwofie said the event was meant to move vendor engagement beyond basic awareness of fraud, ethics and compliance toward deeper and more sustainable partnerships. The overall story is therefore not only about network expansion, but also about how MTN Ghana plans to manage suppliers and delivery risk as it scales.

## Key details

The core operational target is one million homes passed over three years. The article does not specify how many homes will become paying subscribers, nor does it provide a detailed geographic rollout plan, capital expenditure figure or timeline by region. The wording focuses on homes passed, which is a network coverage measure rather than a confirmed customer base.

Blewett linked the fibre expansion to artificial intelligence. He said reliable connectivity to homes and businesses will be needed as AI adoption increases demand for dependable high-speed access. The article presents fibre as critical infrastructure for households and businesses that want to use AI-enabled services, but it does not provide specific AI products, customer use cases or revenue projections.

The company also highlighted 5G readiness. MTN Ghana says it is preparing to leverage its 5G licence to provide modern connectivity and improved speeds. Vendors are expected to support both fibre and 5G deployment, with an emphasis on quality, innovation and integrity.

On vendor relations, Blewett said the relationship must go beyond contractual obligations. He identified trust, open communication, shared objectives and mutual accountability as essential. He also encouraged vendors to raise challenges and risks early, saying the company prefers to hear uncomfortable information in time rather than face unexpected problems later. He added that the partnership should be reciprocal: MTN expects professionalism, integrity and accountability from suppliers, while suppliers should expect fairness, transparency, respect and timely communication from MTN.

Kwofie reinforced the governance message. She said the conference theme, “Building Stronger, Transparent and Sustainable Vendor Partnerships,” reflected a commitment to relationships based on trust and shared accountability. She urged vendors to move beyond a traditional supplier role and take ownership of challenges. She also said success should be judged by changes in conduct and working relationships, not only by discussions. Blewett warned that operational pressure should not become an excuse for unethical conduct and encouraged partners to speak up about practices that threaten integrity.

## Why it matters

The announcement matters because fibre and 5G are foundational infrastructure for digital services. If MTN Ghana expands FTTH as planned, more households and businesses could gain access to higher-speed connectivity. That can support remote work, digital education, e-commerce, cloud services, streaming, government platforms and financial technology. For a bank or financial-services product team, the relevance is indirect but practical: digital banking, payments, customer onboarding, remote servicing and data-heavy products all depend on reliable connectivity. The article does not discuss banking directly, but it shows how telecom infrastructure can shape the environment for digital financial services.

The target also matters because it signals a multi-year vendor and procurement agenda. MTN Ghana is asking suppliers to deliver network expansion while meeting standards of integrity, transparency and accountability. This could affect how vendors bid, report progress, manage risks and handle compliance. For companies that supply network equipment, construction, software or professional services, the message is that delivery capability alone may not be enough; relationship quality and governance are also being emphasized.

There are limits to what the article establishes. It provides a strategic target and management commentary, but not detailed evidence on funding, subscriber demand, construction costs, regulatory approvals or competitive dynamics. The one million homes figure is a goal, not a confirmed outcome. The article also does not explain how MTN Ghana will prioritize locations, whether the buildout will be urban or rural, or how it will measure success beyond homes passed.

For a broad briefing, the main takeaway is that MTN Ghana is positioning fibre and 5G as core platforms for the next phase of digital connectivity, with AI cited as a demand driver. At the same time, the company is publicly linking expansion to vendor ethics and partnership management. That combination suggests execution risk will be as important as network demand: the company needs capable suppliers, but also wants stronger controls around transparency, accountability and conduct.

ghana.headline: Bank of Ghana to introduce upgraded cedi banknotes on December 1
ghana.teaser: New Heritage Series notes will circulate alongside existing legal tender.
ghana.bankAngle: Operational updates for cash handling and distribution.
ghana.imageAlt: Bank of Ghana to introduce upgraded cedi banknotes on December 1
ghana.longSummary:
## The story

The Bank of Ghana has announced the upcoming release of a redesigned family of banknotes, named the Ghana Cedi Heritage Series, with circulation set to begin on December 1, 2026. According to reporting by Techfocus24, the launch event took place on November 12, 2026, at The Bank Square in Accra, with President John Dramani Mahama attending as special guest of honour. The governor of the Bank of Ghana, Dr Johnson Pandit Asiama, presented the new series as a step toward reinforcing public trust in the national currency and ensuring it remains fit for purpose in a changing economy. The existing banknote series will continue to be legal tender and will circulate alongside the new notes for an unspecified period. The central bank also plans to roll out a mobile application called “The Cedi” and a nationwide public education campaign to help citizens recognize the upgraded security features and handle the new notes properly.

## Key details

The Heritage Series incorporates three main upgrades: enhanced security features to deter counterfeiting, improved durability to extend the lifespan of each note, and a more compact physical size intended to make the currency easier to carry and store. The design theme celebrates Ghana’s history and cultural identity, featuring depictions of national heroes, historic sites, monuments, and Adinkra symbols. At the launch, Governor Asiama framed the currency as a representation of the country’s capacity to manage its own monetary affairs through domestic institutions, rather than merely a transactional instrument. He stated that the new series reflects the Bank’s commitment to strengthening confidence in the cedi, protecting its integrity, and meeting the evolving needs of the Ghanaian economy. The accompanying mobile application is intended to provide interactive guidance on the new security elements, while the education campaign will target markets, schools, and community centers across the country. The governor called on the public to treat the currency with care and to view it as an important symbol of national sovereignty.

## Why it matters

Currency redesigns are routine operations for central banks, but they carry practical and symbolic weight. From a practical standpoint, the introduction of more durable and secure notes can reduce the cost of replacing worn or counterfeit bills, lower the risk of fraud in cash transactions, and improve the efficiency of cash-handling systems for banks, businesses, and the public. The shift to smaller dimensions aligns with a global trend toward more portable banknotes, which can also reduce printing and logistics expenses. The decision to keep the current series in circulation avoids the disruption of a sudden demonetization, allowing a gradual transition that is less likely to cause cash shortages or confusion.

Symbolically, embedding national heroes, historic landmarks, and Adinkra symbols into the currency design reinforces a narrative of cultural pride and institutional continuity. In many countries, banknote imagery serves as a daily reminder of shared heritage and state legitimacy. The governor’s emphasis on the cedi as a marker of monetary sovereignty resonates in a region where currency stability has sometimes been challenged by inflation, external shocks, and dollarization pressures. By investing in a modernized, culturally resonant currency, the Bank of Ghana signals its intent to maintain control over monetary policy and to foster public confidence in the domestic financial system.

The planned mobile app and education campaign address a common vulnerability in currency transitions: low public awareness of new security features. When citizens cannot easily distinguish genuine notes from counterfeits, trust erodes and the central bank’s anti-fraud efforts are undermined. A well-executed outreach program, especially one that leverages digital channels, can accelerate adoption and reduce the window of opportunity for counterfeiters. However, the effectiveness of these measures will depend on the reach of the campaign in rural and informal sectors where cash remains dominant and smartphone penetration may be lower.

Overall, the Heritage Series represents a standard but significant central bank maintenance operation. Its success will be measured not only by the technical quality of the notes but by how smoothly the public adapts to them and whether the upgrades contribute to a more resilient and trusted cash ecosystem in Ghana.

ghana.headline: Ghana calls for inclusive emerging technologies to improve lives
ghana.teaser: Government emphasizes AI and digital infrastructure to bridge digital divide.
ghana.whyItMatters: Sets the agenda for digital transformation and tech investment.
ghana.imageAlt: Ghana calls for inclusive emerging technologies to improve lives
ghana.longSummary:
## The story

Ghana has called for the inclusive development and deployment of emerging technologies, particularly artificial intelligence, satellite connectivity and digital infrastructure, to address human needs, bridge the digital divide and create opportunities for all. The call was made by the Minister for Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, Samuel Nartey George, during a panel discussion on emerging technologies at the International Telecommunication Union Plenipotentiary Conference 2026 in Doha, Qatar.

The minister said technology and policy decisions should prioritize people, especially underserved communities, and that technological advancements should translate into meaningful improvements in their lives. He used four hypothetical Ghanaians to illustrate how decisions taken at the global level could directly affect individuals and communities. One example was an AI-powered health service that allows pregnant women to access emergency assistance through basic mobile phones without internet connectivity. According to the minister, the service has enrolled more than 7,000 mothers and expectant mothers at one hospital in Ghana, showing the potential of technology to improve maternal healthcare.

## Key details

On digital connectivity, Mr. George argued that expanding network coverage alone was insufficient. He stressed that access must also be affordable, reliable and meaningful. He called for increased investment in infrastructure, digital skills and local content, particularly in underserved communities.

He also addressed satellite connectivity and spectrum management. He called for equitable access to limited orbital and spectrum resources and cautioned that early satellite deployment should not give operators ownership or exclusive control of space resources.

The minister advocated responsible and accountable AI systems that understand local languages, reflect local realities and guarantee individuals the right to explanations and redress when automated decisions affect their lives.

He called for stronger collaboration among governments, industry, academia and civil society to develop regulatory frameworks that work across borders and reflect the needs of different societies. Ghana has highlighted efforts to strengthen local technological capacity, including the One Million Coders Programme, which has attracted more than 140,000 registrations. The minister said young people must be equipped not only to use technology but also to develop and innovate with it.

He further called for international partnerships that promote local capacity rather than dependency, stressing the importance of increased investment, technology transfer, South-South cooperation and standards that address the priorities of developing countries. He said Ghana is ready to contribute to global efforts to ensure emerging technologies advance inclusion, trust and sustainable digital development.

## Why it matters

Ghana’s position reflects a broader concern about how emerging technologies are designed, funded and governed. The minister’s emphasis on people-centered development suggests that digital transformation strategies should consider the needs of underserved groups rather than assuming that access alone is enough.

The AI health example is one of the more concrete illustrations in the article. It points to how AI could support maternal healthcare through basic mobile phones, though the minister’s account is an example presented during a panel discussion and not yet proof of large-scale deployment. The figure of more than 7,000 enrolled mothers at one hospital indicates early practical use, but the article does not provide broader evidence about effectiveness or outcomes.

The discussion of connectivity and spectrum adds a policy dimension. Expanding coverage is not only a technical issue, because affordability, reliability and meaningful use matter. Similarly, satellite deployment and spectrum allocation raise questions about equity and control. Ghana’s caution about exclusive control suggests concern that new frontiers could concentrate power among a few operators or states.

The call for accountable AI, local languages and redress is significant because it moves beyond adoption debates into questions of design and rights. The minister’s argument that Africa should help shape AI rather than only react to it frames inclusion as a governance challenge. The One Million Coders Programme and international partnership language reinforce that local capacity building is seen as important for reducing dependency.

For stakeholders, the key takeaway is that Ghana views inclusive emerging technology as a priority for national digital policy. The country is using its role in international forums to press for attention to underserved communities, local content, skills and responsible innovation. The next steps would depend on how these calls translate into national policy, regulation and implementation.
